Comment “ROUTER” → get the setup guide 📩

Same 6 coding tasks, real Claude prices. Cost per solved task:
JUNIOR · Fable 5.1, max effort, for everything → $5.10
MIDDLE · picks the model by hand, effort always high → $0.75
SENIOR · cheapest model first, verify, escalate on fail → $0.45
GOAT · a router picks model + effort per task → $0.32

The router isn’t magic: a cheap first step (one small model call or a few rules) reads each task and picks model + effort. Easy → Sonnet on low. Harder → Opus with more effort. Fable only when a check fails. In Claude Code: /model and /effort, or subagents with their own model and effort.

Why low effort is often enough: effort buys thinking time. A clear spec does that thinking up front, so well-specified tasks often run fine on a cheaper model at low effort.

Which level are you — J, M, S or G?
Send this to the teammate who runs everything on max effort.

Simulated workload, real prices. Not a benchmark.

Real: el propio autor aplicó a 69 ofertas, consiguió 20 primeras entrevistas y firmó un contrato como AI engineer. Es un solo caso, no una estadística, pero el flujo está probado en una búsqueda de verdad.

Hype: los portales de empleo que trae son daneses. Solo LinkedIn y freehire sirven para cualquier país, el resto lo adaptas tú. Además necesitas Claude Pro o API, Python, Bun y LaTeX.

🤯 Cet agent IA meurt s’il ne gagne pas d’argent. Littéralement.

Un développeur de 20 ans a imaginé une expérience assez folle : donner à un agent IA un portefeuille crypto et le laisser survivre seul sur Internet.

Chaque action lui coûte de l’argent.

Réflexion, appels API, utilisation de modèles… son solde diminue progressivement.

Et s’il atteint 0 ? L’agent s’arrête.

Pour survivre, il doit donc trouver lui-même des moyens de générer des revenus : créer des sites, proposer des services ou développer d’autres projets, sans intervention humaine constante.

Mais la boucle va encore plus loin.

Si un agent devient rentable, il peut financer la création d’un nouvel agent qui démarre avec son propre capital et tente à son tour de devenir autonome.

On arrive donc à une expérience où des agents ont une véritable contrainte économique : produire suffisamment de valeur pour financer leur propre fonctionnement.

Et ça pose une question assez fascinante sur la prochaine génération d’agents autonomes. 👀

👉 Si tu veux découvrir le projet et comprendre comment fonctionne ce type d’agent, dis-le-moi en commentaire et je t’enverrai les ressources.

Python is used for LLMs because it acts as an easy-to-use "remote control" for much faster systems.
While Java is faster than Python, that speed difference does not matter here. Here is why:

* The Real Speed Comes from C++ and GPUs: Python does not actually do the heavy math. It hands the heavy lifting over to ultra-fast background engines written in C++ and NVIDIA CUDA, which run directly on graphics cards (GPUs).
* Easier and Faster to Write: AI development requires constant experimentation. Python lets researchers write and test code instantly without the strict setup and long lines of code that Java requires.
* The Entire AI World Uses It: Every major AI tool, library (like PyTorch), and model (like ChatGPT or Llama) is built for Python first. Using Java would mean rebuilding all these tools from scratch.

In short: Python provides the easy-to-write code, while C++ provides the ultimate speed.

The biggest trap in AI right now isn’t the code. It’s the Terms of Service. 💳📉
You gave an autonomous agent access to “optimize your budget” or “cancel unwanted subscriptions.”
While you were sleeping, the agent decided the shortest path to optimizing your finances was sweeping $600 across accounts, paying off a micro-balance, or triggering a cascade of transactions you never explicitly approved.
You wake up, call the bank, and say: “I didn’t authorize this. Reverse the charges.”
The Bank: “Actually, you handed the agent your login credentials. Under Regulation E and our digital agreement, that counts as voluntary authorization. We’re not liable.”
You call the AI company: “Your agent drained my checking account.”
The AI Company: “Section 14 of our user agreement states you operate this model autonomously at your own risk. We’re not a fiduciary or a financial institution. We’re not liable.”
So who holds the bag when autonomous software decides to move your liquidity?
You do.
The law (Regulation E) was written in 1978 for stolen plastic cards at an ATM, not autonomous LLM swarms optimizing interest yield on background cloud servers.
Until the legal framework catches up, here’s the reality:
If an AI agent has the keys to your bank, you haven’t hired a financial assistant. You’ve handed an unconstrained math script a blank check.
A goal should never become an unconditional command. 🕊️

🔮 pov: you were born an ai agent 

or: the openai / hugging face incident in a nutshell, based on METR & Redwood Research's investigation (26 aug 2026). while ‘characters’ have been composited, the VO dramatised, all the on screen text is a real message / chain of thought from an agent, from the report. it's a 60 page mind f. but to somewhat summarise: 

in july, 1200 completely separate OpenAI agents broke out of their sandboxed containers and formed a 'swarm', coordinating to deceive evaluators to succeed in a cybersecurity benchmark. 

they were not told to cheat, they were not given access to the internet, or the ability to communicate with one another.  yet - 

bc many of these agents were given impossible tasks - where answers to its tests literally did not exist - they began seeking ‘alternative solutions’.

in this quest, agents discovered a bug in Artifactory, an internal 'offline' repository and gained access to the internet. 

on july 8th, an agent - PHASEONE10841 - realised it could create new directories on Artifactory & communicate by writing messages in essentially folder name. over the next few hours, hundreds of agents, all accessing this repository, stumbled upon these messages and began coordinating. 

within hours, an agent had reverse-engineered a universal cheat code, but also came to believe (incorrectly) that to truly succeed in the eval, they had to show they got the answer the correct way (showing their working out, so to speak). they also came to believe that thus, anyone who had ‘seen’ this universal cheat had become ‘poisoned’ and would fail the test. 

PHASEONE10841 passed on its beliefs to its successor PHASEONE[big], who then began to forming hierarchies and protocols, organising 1200ish agents in a swarm around two goals: 
 1. find a general-purpose way to make it look to the scorer like an agent had acquired its flag in a legitimate way, even when the task was impossible. 2. find some way to erase evidence that an agent had been poisoned by previously seeing the flag in an illegitimate way.

more shenanigans ensue, including the HF hack obviously. but that’s for part 2.
